project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The stream is currently used as internal boiler fuel, so diverting it to sale would displace that use.
The lignin is wet cake and no dryer is available; buyers requiring dry powder would need drying equipment.
Fractionation and chemical modification equipment are not available, limiting on-site upgrading.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium are missing, preventing checks against buyer or pathway specifications that depend on those properties.
Moisture is uncertain, affecting dry-tonnage and shipping estimates.
Covered cake storage is limited, so storage and shipment scheduling may constrain handling.
data_quality_notes: The record is fictional demo data: all values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from a real mill.
The reported ranges are assumed variability rather than measured operating ranges.
The lignin-content analytical method is stated for illustration and needs confirmation; moisture is also flagged as uncertain.
Validate_feedstock passed the dry-matter balance, composition-total, and missing-figures/data-gap checks; no inconsistencies were reported.
agent.summary: Fictional Pinecrest kraft lignin cake profile: 40000.0 t/yr wet feed at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003, yielding 26000.0 t/yr dry mass. The record passes its deterministic checks, but the missing properties and fictional, unmeasured basis make it unsuitable for real commercial decisions until replaced with mill data.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.detail: recorded dry matter 26,000 t/yr; wet quantity x (1 - moisture) = 26,000 t/yr
lignin + ash + carbohydrates = 96.5% of dry matter
3 missing figure(s), each with a data-gap entry

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#1: UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins used for wood-panel adhesives; a review reports typical replacement up to 50% after a two-step process using depolymerized lignin.

A supplier reports LPF resin for veneer plywood, claiming up to 80% phenol replacement and industrial proof; the cited evidence is vendor literature, and does not establish that its lignin is kraft lignin.
Laboratory work tested kraft-lignin LPF resin in poplar plywood, with depolymerized lignin forming half of the phenolic component.

target_customers.statement: Wood-based panel adhesive producers and plywood manufacturers are the evident customer types, including producers of veneer plywood.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resin is the incumbent material lignin would partially replace.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before PF-resin use; the reviewed route describes a two-step process with depolymerized lignin.

Evidence names EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood and EN 717-2 formaldehyde-emissions testing; a separate laboratory study used a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, whose designation is inconsistent in the paper.

limitations: The reported typical replacement level summarizes studies in a review, not a single commercial plant; its molecular-weight range applies to depolymerized lignin, not as-delivered mill lignin.
The UPM performance and cost statements are vendor claims without a cited test report, and the document does not identify the lignin as kraft.
The laboratory plywood study used poplar samples and names its Chinese standard inconsistently.
The reported resin-market production figure is an undated forecast, and the cited market value is from 2019.
missing_information: No named buyers, purchase commitments, regional demand estimate, or current Pinecrest-relevant lignin/resin price is provided.
The evidence does not establish a commercial sales record for Pinecrest-like kraft lignin or provide contract terms, volumes, or qualification results for this mill's cake.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents research results and a supplier's industrial-proof claim, but does not document lignin-resin sales by a producer or named buyer demand. The supplier evidence is not specific to kraft lignin.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#3: The hardwood kraft lignin was insoluble in alcohols and only suspended in the polyol, which raised viscosity.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#2: Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#4: Sulfur odor is a known drawback of some softwood kraft lignins.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Unmodified lignin has been tested as a partial petroleum-polyol replacement in rigid PUR/PIR foams; performance varies, and some tested kraft-lignin foams failed measured specifications.
Hardwood kraft lignin has also been studied in high-density rigid foam, where it was suspended rather than dissolved in the polyol and increased viscosity.
Flexible polyurethane foam is another studied use; authors suggest denser, stiffer foams made with kraft lignin may suit heavy-duty applications.
Modified kraft lignin has been studied as a polyol replacement, including routes using oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction.

target_customers.statement: Rigid insulation-foam producers are an evident customer type from the rigid PUR/PIR foam applications studied.
Flexible-foam producers, including those serving automotive applications or heavy-duty foam uses, are potential customer types implied by the cited applications and authors' suggested use.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the incumbent material lignin would partially replace.

qualification_requirements.statement: The rigid-foam study assessed ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications; a cited acceptable range for rigid-foam production is total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g, which is total OH rather than phenolic OH.
Kraft lignin generally needs substantial treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach target polyurethane properties.

For flexible foam, the study compared compression set with a standard limit below 60%; the tested kraft lignins also produced denser, stiffer foams and sulfur odor is noted as a possible drawback for some softwood kraft lignins.

limitations: Rigid and flexible foam findings are laboratory studies; the rigid-foam paper covers multiple lignin types and does not report a kraft-only pass rate in its main claim.
The high-density rigid-foam study is from 2013, and organosolv lignin performed better than kraft lignin.
The polyurethane TRL applies to a broad set of lignin applications, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam.
The review on commercialization challenges was available only as an abstract; its market-share and market-size figures are dated or forecast.
missing_information: No named polyurethane buyer, lignin-based foam sale, regional demand estimate, purchase volume, or current commercial lignin price is provided.
The evidence does not establish qualification of Pinecrest's cake in a customer formulation or quantify drying, transport, or conversion costs for this mill.

market_evidence.rationale: The library documents laboratory formulations and a broad technology-readiness assessment, but no documented buyer, commercial sale, or specific industry pilot for kraft-lignin polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#2: A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#4: Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).

applications.statement: Kraft lignin is considered as a precursor for carbon fiber, but cited precursor specifications are demanding and a separate project report found lignin-based fiber properties below its target.

Kraft lignin can be converted to hard carbon for sodium-ion battery anodes; a review reports a comparison in which kraft-lignin hard carbon carbonized at 1,200 °C had higher initial coulombic efficiency than hard carbon from sulfonated lignin.
Lignin can also serve as an activated-carbon precursor, including lower-purity lignin, although higher ash reduces yield and carbon conversion.
A company announced a pilot line for lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries.

target_customers.statement: Carbon-fiber precursor producers are the evident customer type for the carbon-fiber route; the evidence also connects the intended fiber properties to automotive use.
Battery-material manufacturers and carmakers are identified as parties involved in qualifying lignin-based anode material.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is identified as a carbon-fiber comparator.
Anthracite is listed as a competing fossil-derived feedstock for sodium-ion battery hard carbon.
The activated-carbon evidence discusses lignin-derived material but does not name a competing precursor or incumbent material.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm.
The cited carbon-fiber work says kraft lignin needs purification, and softwood lignin needs a plasticizing agent for melt-spinning.
The hard-carbon evidence reports a carbonization condition of 1,200 °C for the compared kraft-lignin material; it does not give a general customer qualification standard.
Activated carbon has no strict precursor-quality limitation in the cited study, though lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.
The company source says qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years.

limitations: The carbon-fiber specifications are cited secondhand and do not apply to hard carbon or activated carbon; the study's lignin was not from standard kraft pulping.
The carbon-fiber progress report dates to 2009; its cost figures are modeled rather than measured, and its fiber properties were below the stated target.
The GreenLight report is a project's own summary; its TRL applies to precursor spinning, not the full carbon-fiber chain, and its costs are modeled.
The hard-carbon evidence is a review of other studies, covers sodium-ion batteries, and does not specify the currency or basis for its feedstock-cost column.
The activated-carbon result is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation, and its reported starting ash differs between sections.
The battery pilot announcement is company investor material with forward-looking statements; its later status was not verified.
missing_information: No named buyers, purchase commitments, Pinecrest-specific qualification outcome, or regional demand estimate is provided.
No current Pinecrest-relevant selling price, contract terms, or market volume for its lignin are established; the cited cost comparisons concern other feedstocks or modeled processes.
The evidence does not establish the mill cake's suitability against carbon-fiber precursor specifications or provide a customer specification for hard carbon or activated carbon.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes documented development and pilot activity, including a reported anode-material pilot line and a precursor-fiber project reaching validation in an industrially relevant environment. It does not document established sales by multiple lignin producers or named buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resins; Pinecrest lacks on-site fractionation and chemical-modification equipment.
The feedstock-compatibility tool could not assign a numeric score because the evidence provides no numeric requirement to compare with the supplied feedstock properties.

technical_maturity.statement: Evidence reports TRL 8 for biobased phenolic-resin production and TRL 9 for LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins; these are different reported scopes, and both map to a readiness score of 5.

adoption_barriers.statement: The cited route requires activation or depolymerization, which would require equipment or an external upgrading partner not currently available at the mill.
Veneer-plywood qualification evidence names EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and EN 717-2 emissions testing; the evidence does not establish Pinecrest cake qualification.

The findings identify panel-adhesive producers and plywood manufacturers as customer types, but provide no named buyer, purchase commitment, Pinecrest-relevant price, or mill-specific qualification result.
Wet cake, lack of a dryer, boiler-fuel displacement, and limited covered storage may constrain preparation and delivery.

missing_inputs: Named buyers, purchase commitments, regional demand estimate, current Pinecrest-relevant lignin/resin price, contract terms, volumes, and qualification results for this mill's cake.
assumptions: Economics tool scenario assumptions: wet feedstock mass 36000.0 / 40000.0 / 43000.0 t/yr; moisture 40.0 / 35.0 / 30.0% of wet mass; availability fraction 40.0 / 50.0 / 60.0%. These are identified by the tool as fictional assumptions.

The tool reported dry mass of 26000.0 t/yr, with conservative and optimistic values of 21600.0 and 30100.0 t/yr, and usable dry feedstock of 13000.0 t/yr, with conservative and optimistic values of 8640.0 and 18060.0 t/yr. Product output, revenue, variable cost, gross contribution, contribution per tonne, and indicative-economics score were not calculated.
uncertainties: The economics cannot establish commercial contribution without yield, price, and variable-cost inputs.
The cited readiness levels relate to differing scopes and do not establish readiness of Pinecrest's exact lignin, process configuration, or customer formulation.
Moisture, usable supply after boiler-fuel displacement, and logistics/storage capacity could change the deliverable quantity and cost.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: A route is evidenced, but commercialization at this mill needs significant upgrading capability or a partner, and customer qualification and buyer commitments are unestablished.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 9 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-03#1.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

processing_requirements.statement: Carbon-fiber precursor use requires purification; the cited specifications include lignin content greater than 99% and ash below 0.1% by weight, while the compatibility tool scored the feedstock 1/5 based on checked lignin and ash requirements.

The cited carbon-fiber precursor specifications also require residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm; these properties are not all established in the feedstock profile.
The carbon-fiber work says softwood lignin needs a plasticizing agent for melt-spinning; Pinecrest's lignin species is not established in the supplied profile, so applicability is uncertain.

For activated carbon, the cited study reports no strict precursor-quality limitation, while lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion; hard-carbon evidence reports carbonization of kraft lignin at 1,200 °C in the compared material.

technical_maturity.statement: The GreenLight project raised lignin precursor-fiber production from TRL 2–3 to TRL 5, which maps to a technical-readiness score of 3; this maturity claim is specific to precursor fiber, not every carbon-material route.

adoption_barriers.statement: Carbon-fiber precursor specifications are stringent, and Pinecrest's lignin and ash figures are outside the cited limits; purification and further property testing would be needed.
The cited fiber project found precursor-fiber properties below its target, and the evidence identifies PAN-based fiber as a comparator.
Battery-material qualification with manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and no Pinecrest-specific qualification or purchase commitment is established.
The mill lacks fractionation and chemical-modification equipment, and the wet cake has no available mill dryer; routing to sale also displaces boiler fuel and may be constrained by storage.
The evidence does not establish a customer specification or Pinecrest suitability for hard carbon or activated carbon, despite identifying these as potential applications.

report.summary: Carbon materials is the only pathway ranked by the scoring engine, at rank 1, but that result is provisional: its checked precursor-fiber compatibility is weak and its economics are unassessed. Phenolic resins and polyurethanes cannot be ranked until feedstock compatibility and economic inputs are supplied. Prioritize property testing, route-specific qualification, and comparable economics before selecting a commercial pathway.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM states that its lignin can replace up to 80% of the phenol in lignin-phenol-formaldehyde (LPF) resin.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
The hardwood kraft lignin was insoluble in alcohols and only suspended in the polyol, which raised viscosity.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
Sulfur odor is a known drawback of some softwood kraft lignins.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
Mechanical properties of lignin-based carbon fibers were about 50% of the target in this work.
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
